faq.q: What scatters the light in the sky?
faq.a: The gas molecules of the air itself, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. They are far smaller than a wavelength of light, which is why they scatter short blue waves so much more than long red ones.
asks: Which particles cause the blue sky?

faq.q: Why does blue light scatter more than red?
faq.a: Scattering by tiny molecules gets much stronger as the wavelength gets shorter. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, so it is scattered roughly five times more.

faq.q: Why is the sky not violet?
faq.a: Violet does scatter even more than blue, but sunlight contains less violet, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are much less sensitive to violet. So the mix we see looks blue.
asks: If violet scatters most, why isn't the sky purple?

faq.q: Is sunlight really made of colours?
faq.a: Yes. White sunlight is a mix of all the colours from red to violet. A prism or a rainbow splits it so you can see them.

faq.q: Is the sky blue because it reflects the sea?
faq.a: No. The sky is just as blue over deserts far from any sea. The blue comes from air scattering sunlight; in fact the sea looks blue partly because it reflects the sky.
asks: Does the ocean make the sky blue?

facts: Rayleigh scattering is named after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, who explained it in the 1870s.
Blue light at about 450 nanometres is scattered roughly five times more than red light at about 700 nanometres.
On the Moon, which has almost no air, the sky looks black even in daytime.

quiz.show: Why is the daytime sky black on the Moon?

options.show: The Moon is too far from the Sun

options.say: There is no air to scatter sunlight

quiz.why: The blue sky is sunlight scattered by air molecules. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so nothing scatters the light and the sky stays black.

wrong.0: The Moon is about as far from the Sun as Earth is, and its ground is brightly lit.
wrong.2: The dust is on the ground; the sky above is black because there is no air to scatter light.
